'''''Sansevieria''''' is a historically recognized genus of [[flowering plant]]s, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia, now included in the genus '''''[[Dracaena (plant)|Dracaena]]''''' on the basis of [[Molecular phylogenetics|molecular phylogenetic]] studies.<ref name="hisako"/><ref>{{citation |last=Stevens |first=P.F. |date=2001{{ndash}}2012 |title=Angiosperm Phylogeny Website: Asparagales: Nolinoideae |url=https://www.mobot.org/mobot/research/apweb/orders/asparagalesweb.htm#Ruscaceae }}</ref><ref name=LuMord14/> Common names for the 70 or so species formerly placed in the genus include '''mother-in-law's tongue, devil's tongue, [[jinn]]'s tongue, bow string hemp, [[snake plant]]''' and '''snake tongue'''.<ref>{{cite book | last = Mbugua
| first = P. K. |author2=D. M. Moore  | editor = L. J. G. van der Maesen |editor2=M. van der Burgt |editor3=J. M. van Medenbach de Rooy | title = The Biodiversity of African Plants | type = hardcover | edition = 1st | chapter = Taxonomic studies of the genus Sansevieria (Dracaenaceae) | year = 1996 | page = 880| doi = 10.1007/978-94-009-0285-5_62 | isbn = 978-94-010-6613-6 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-0285-5_62}}</ref> In the [[APG III system|APG III classification system]], ''Dracaena'' is placed in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asparagaceae]], subfamily Convallarioideae (formerly subfamily Nolinoideae<ref name="APweb">Stevens, P.F. (2001 onwards). [https://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/research/APweb/orders/asparagalesweb.htm#Convallarioideae "7. Convallarioideae Herbert"]. ''Angiosperm Phylogeny Website''. Retrieved 2025-08-10.</ref>); before that it was placed in family Ruscaceae.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Chase |first1=M.W. |last2=Reveal |first2=J.L. |last3=Fay |first3=M.F. |year=2009 |title=A subfamilial classification for the expanded asparagalean families Amaryllidaceae, Asparagaceae and Xanthorrhoeaceae |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=161 |issue=2 |pages=132–136 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2009.00999.x|name-list-style=amp |doi-access=free }}</ref> It has also been placed in the former family Dracaenaceae.

==Description==
There is great variation within the species formerly placed in the [[genus]]; they range from [[succulent plant|succulent]] [[xerophyte|desert plants]] such as ''[[Dracaena pinguicula]]'' to thinner leafed tropical plants such as ''[[Dracaena trifasciata]]''. Plants often form dense clumps from a spreading [[rhizome]] or [[stolon]]s.<ref name="STOVER">{{cite book |last= Stover |first= Hermine |title= The Sansevieria Book |year= 1983|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K6V3GQAACAAJ}}</ref><ref name="JUAN">{{cite book |last= Chahinian |first= B. Juan |title= The Splendid Sansevieria: An Account of the Species |year= 2005 |publisher= B. Juan Chahinian |isbn= 987-43-9250-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kSt6GQAACAAJ}}</ref>

===Foliage===
The leaves of former ''Sansevieria'' species are typically arranged in a rosette around the [[Apical meristem|growing point]], although some species are [[Phyllotaxis|distichous]]. There is a great variation in foliage form. All former species can be divided into one of two basic categories based on their leaves: hard leaved and soft-leaved species. Typically, hard-leaved species originate from arid climates, while soft-leaved species originate from tropical and subtropical regions.<ref name = "STOVER"/> Hard leaved species have a number of adaptations for surviving dry regions. These include thick, succulent leaves for storing water and thick leaf [[plant cuticle|cuticles]] for reducing moisture loss. These leaves may be cylindrical to reduce surface area and are generally shorter than those of their soft leafed tropical counterparts, which are wide and strap-like.<ref name = "STOVER"/>

===Flowers===
The [[flower]]s of former ''Sansevieria'' species are usually greenish-white, also rose, lilac-red, brownish, produced on a simple or branched [[raceme]]. The [[fruit]] is a red or orange [[Berry (botany)|berry]]. In nature, they are pollinated by moths, but both flowering and fruiting are erratic and few seeds are produced.<ref name = "STOVER"/><ref name = "JUAN"/> The raceme is derived from the [[apical meristem]], and a flowered shoot will no longer produce new leaves. Unlike plants such as [[agave]] which [[Semelparity and iteroparity#Semelparity|die after flowering]], a bloomed shoot will simply cease to produce new leaves. The flowered shoot continues to grow by producing plantlets via its [[rhizomes]] or [[stolons]].

==Taxonomy==
The genus name ''Sansevieria'' honors [[Italy|Italian]] scientist and inventor [[Raimondo di Sangro]] (1710–1771), Prince of [[San Severo]].<ref name= "Coombes">Coombes, Allen J. (2012). "The A to Z of Plant Names". Timber Press. {{ISBN|9781604691962}} (hardback).  pp 265</ref><ref name= "gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 339</ref> The genus was originally named ''Sanseverinia'' by [[Vincenzo Petagna]] in 1787,<ref name=IPNI_62517-3>{{cite web |title=Plant Name Details for ''Sansevieria'' Thunb. |work=[[International Plant Names Index|The International Plant Names Index]] |url=https://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=62517-3 |access-date=2018-07-15 }}</ref> to honor his patron Pietro Antonio Sanseverino, Count of Chiaromonte (1724–1771), in whose garden Petagna had seen the plant.<ref name=Mara73>{{Cite journal |last1=Marais |first1=W. |date=1973 |title=(350) Proposal to Amend the Entry of 1100. Sanseviera in the List of Nomina Generica Conservanda |journal=Taxon |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=158–159 |doi=10.2307/1218069 |jstor=1218069 }}</ref> In 1794, [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] used the name ''Sansevieria''.<ref name=IPNI_62517-3/><ref>{{citation |mode=cs1|contribution=Section S |title=ICN: Appendix IIIA Nomina Generica Conservanda et Rejicienda |contribution-url=http://www.ibot.sav.sk/icbn/frameset/0104AppendixIIIANGEs002.htm#s |access-date=2018-07-15 }}</ref> It is not clear whether Thunberg's name was intended to be new, or was a typographical error for Petagna's name.<ref name=Mara73/> "''Sansevieria'' <small>Thunb.</small>" is a [[conserved name]] in the [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants]], notwithstanding arguments that the author should be given as Petagna.<ref name=Mara73/><ref name=MenaDeLuDelG13>{{Citation |last1=Menale |first1=Bruno |last2=De Luca |first2=Paolo |last3=Del Guacchio |first3=Emanuele |date=2013 |title=A plea to restore Petagna's authorship for the genus Sansevieria, nom. cons. (Liliaceae) |journal=Taxon |volume=62 |issue=2 |pages=387–390 |doi=10.12705/622.7 |jstor=taxon.62.2.387 |name-list-style=amp }}</ref> The spellings "''Sanseveria''" and "''Sanseviera''" are commonly seen as well, the confusion deriving from alternate spellings of the Italian place name.{{Citation needed|date=July 2018}}

[[Molecular phylogenetics|Molecular phylogenetic]] studies showed that ''Sansevieria'' was nested within ''[[Dracaena (plant)|Dracaena]]'', rendering the latter [[Paraphyly|paraphyletic]] unless ''Dracaena'' was expanded to include the species formerly placed in ''Sansevieria''.<ref name=LuMord14>{{Citation |last1=Lu |first1=Pei-Luen |last2=Morden |first2=Clifford W. |date=2014 |title=Phylogenetic Relationships among Dracaenoid Genera (Asparagaceae: Nolinoideae) Inferred from Chloroplast DNA Loci |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=90–104 |doi=10.1600/036364414X678035 |s2cid=86171270 |name-list-style=amp }}</ref>

===Sections===
As of 2015, the genus was subdivided into three sections, one of which was further subdivided into three subsections:<ref>Mansfeld, P.A. ''Die Systematik der Gattung Sansevieria (Asparagaceae)''. Sansevieria Online 3(1). 2015.</ref>
* sect. ''Sansevieria'' 
** subsect. ''Sansevieria''
** subsect. ''Hastifolia''
** subsect. ''Solonifera''
* sect. ''Dracomima''
* sect. ''Cephalantha''

==Uses==

===Rope and traditional uses===
In Africa, the leaves of former ''Sansevieria'' species are used for [[Natural fiber|fiber]] production;<ref>{{cite book | last = Kirby | first = F. Vaughan |title = Sport in East Central Africa: Being An Account of Hunting Trips in Portuguese And Other Districts of East Central Africa | url = https://archive.org/details/sportineastcentr00kirb | year = 1899 }}</ref> in some species, e.g. ''[[Dracaena hanningtonii]]'', the plant's sap has antiseptic qualities, and the leaves are used for bandages in traditional [[first aid]].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Chinasa|first1=EC |last2=Obodoike |first2=EC |last3=Chhukwuemeka |first3=ES |year=2011 |title=Evaluation of anti-inflammatory property of the leaves of Sansevieria liberica ger. and labr. (fam: Dracaenaceae). |journal=Asian Pac J Trop Med |volume=4|issue=10 |pages=791–5 |doi=10.1016/S1995-7645(11)60195-8|pmid=22014734 |name-list-style=amp|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Ornamental purposes===
[[Image:snake plant.jpg|thumb|right|A variegated cultivar of ''[[Dracaena trifasciata]]'' (namely 'Laurentii'), the most common species in cultivation]]
Several former ''Sansevieria'' species are popular [[houseplant]]s in temperate regions, with ''[[Dracaena trifasciata]]'' the most widely sold; numerous [[cultivar]]s are available. In China, the plant is usually kept potted in a pot often ornamented with dragons and phoenixes.<ref name="about-garden.com">{{Cite web|url=https://www.about-garden.com/a/en/1919-sansevieria-trifasciata-snake-plant/|title=Sansevieria trifasciata|website=About-garden.com}}</ref> Growth is comparatively slow and the plant will last for many years. There are two main varieties: wild type sansevierias have stiff, erect, scattered, lance-shaped leaves while the bird's nest sansevierias grow in rosettes. As houseplants, sansevierias thrive on warmth and bright light, but will also tolerate shade. They can rot from over-watering, so it is important that they are potted in well-drained soil, and not over-watered.  They need to be re-potted or split at the root from time to time because they will sometimes grow so large that they break the pot they are growing in.

In Korea, potted sansevierias are commonly presented as a gift during opening ceremonies of businesses or other auspicious events.
In Barbados, sansevieria is also popularly referred to as the "money plant", with the belief that the person having it will always have money.  The belief seems to be based on an association of the color (green) with the US bills. {{citation needed|date=January 2012}}

Other former ''Sansevieria'' species are less common in cultivation. Another species is ''[[Sansevieria cylindrica]]'', which has leaves which look quite different from ''D. trifasciata'', but is equally tough.<ref name="McDonald2012" />

Plants can be propagated by seed, leaf-cutting, and division. Seeds are rarely used, as plants can normally be grown much faster from cuttings or divisions. As many cultivars are periclinal [[Chimera (plant)|chimeras]], they do not come true to type from leaf cuttings, and therefore must be propagated by rhizome division to retain the variegation.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/foliage/folnotes/sansevie.htm |title=Sansevieria Production Guide |first1=R.W. |last1=Henley |first2=A.R. |last2=Chase |first3=L.S. |last3=Osborne |publisher=University of Florida, IFAS}}</ref> Plants that revert when propagated from a leaf cutting due to being periclinal chimeras will usually revert to the closest stable non-variagated cultivar to that of the plant the leaf cutting was from.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Ultimate Guide to Propagating Sansevieria Successfully From Leaf Cuttings |url=https://lebotanist.com.au/blogs/greenerygazette/the-ultimate-guide-to-propagating-sansevieria-successfully-from-leaf-cuttings |website=Le Botanist |access-date=12 March 2025}}</ref>

===Scenery in film and television===
Sansevierias have frequently been used as a set decoration in many films and TV shows, both in Hollywood and internationally, since at least the 1930s, including ''[[Being John Malkovich]]'', ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]'', ''[[Duck Soup (1933 film)|Duck Soup]]'', ''[[Groundhog Day (film)|Groundhog Day]]'', ''[[Homegrown (1998 film)|Homegrown]]'', ''[[The Paper (film)|The Paper]]'', and ''[[These Final Hours]]''.

===Air purification===
According to a [[NASA Clean Air Study]], along with other plants such as [[Epipremnum aureum|golden pothos]] (''Epipremnum aureum'') and [[Dracaena fragrans|corn plant]] (''Dracaena fragrans''), ''[[Dracaena trifasciata]]'' is capable of purifying air by removing some pollutants such as [[formaldehyde]], [[xylene]], and [[toluene]].<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19930073077.pdf | title = Interior Landscape Plants for Indoor Air Pollution Abatement | date = 15 September 1989 | publisher = NASA | last1 = Wolverton | first1 = B. C. | last2 = Johnson | first2 = Anne | last3 = Bounds | first3 = Keith }}</ref> Sansevierias use the [[crassulacean acid metabolism]] process,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gilman|first1=I.S.|last2=Smith|first2=J.A.C.|last3=Holtum|first3=J.A.M.|last4=Sage|first4=R.F.|last5=Silvera|first5=K.|last6=Winter|first6=K.|last7=Edwards|first7=E.J.|pmid=37698538|title=The CAM lineages of planet Earth|journal=Annals of Biology|volume=132|issue=4|pages=627–654|doi=10.1093/aob/mcad135|doi-access=free|year=2023|pmc=10799995 }}</ref> which absorbs carbon dioxide at night, although oxygen is released during daylight. Nighttime absorption of {{chem2|CO2}} purportedly makes them especially suitable bedroom plants.{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} However, since the leaves are potentially poisonous if ingested, they are not usually recommended for children's bedrooms.{{citation needed|date=June 2024}}

===Feng shui===
According to [[feng shui]], because the leaves of sansevierias grow upwards, the plants can be used for feng shui purposes.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fengshuipalace.com/fs101/faq.shtml |title=faq |publisher=feng shui palace |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180715123149/http://www.fengshuipalace.com/fs101/faq.shtml |archive-date=2018-07-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.portlandnursery.com/plants/houseplantPicks/sansevieria-cylindrica.shtml |title=SANSEVIERIA CYLINDRICA |publisher=[[Portland Nursery]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100618001302/http://www.portlandnursery.com/plants/houseplantPicks/sansevieria-cylindrica.shtml |archive-date=2010-06-18 |quote=Using Feng Shui principles, the Sansevieria is used to bring good fortune into the home, while warding off evil spirits.}}</ref> Some believe that having sansevierias near children helps reduce coarseness, although care must be taken to ensure the child cannot reach the plant's poisonous leaves.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.womanspassions.com/articles/2149.html |title=Feng Shui and indoor plants |access-date=2010-04-19 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527171511/http://www.womanspassions.com/articles/2149.html |archive-date=27 May 2010 }}</ref> Others recommend placing pots near the toilet tank to counter the drain-down vibrations.<ref>{{cite book |last= Englebert |first= Clear |title=Bedroom Feng Shui |publisher= Crossing Press |year= 2001 |page= 143| isbn= 1-58091-109-9}}</ref>
